w2-no-new-false-negatives.title: Did the fix buy its precision by going blind?
w2-no-new-false-negatives.imperative: The fix makes the lint stop flagging things. That is the direction where a false NEGATIVE hides: if skipping redirect-shaped tokens or refusing to judge an unusable interpreter is too broad, genuinely vacuous checks now pass silently, which is worse than the false positives it removed. Construct real zero-collect defects in several shapes -- a selector matching nothing with a redirect present, one without, one behind a pipe, one with an interpreter that does have pytest -- and confirm each is still caught. Say plainly which shapes the lint now declines to judge.
w2-no-new-false-negatives.finding:
Built 7 real zero-collect shapes and ran validate() directly (repro script preserved at /tmp/w2_shapes.py): (A) direct `python -m pytest -k <zero-selector>` no redirect -- CAUGHT. (B) same with `2>/dev/null` appended, no pipe -- CAUGHT. (C) idiom-shaped, genuinely zero, behind a pipe -- CAUGHT. (D) bare `pytest ...` (no `-m`), run under an interpreter that HAS pytest -- CAUGHT. (E) `python3 -m pytest ...` where python3 lacks pytest, genuinely zero -- NOT caught (expected/by-design: undecidable, not a fault). (F) pytest piped INTO from an upstream command -- CAUGHT. (G) real selector control -- correctly not flagged. Six of seven behave as intended.

But (D)'s safety is conditional, and testing it the way the round-1 false-positive was actually discovered exposes a real gap: `_resolve_interpreter(None)` (the bare-`pytest`, no-`-m` case) falls back to `named or sys.executable` -- i.e. whichever python is running validate_spine.py ITSELF, exactly the fallback z2 was supposed to eliminate. z2 only fixed the case where the check's command TEXT names an interpreter (`-m pytest`); a bare `pytest` command names no interpreter at all, so `_resolve_interpreter` silently reuses sys.executable for it, unconditionally, same as before this rework.

Reproduced live end-to-end via the actual CLI, not just the library call: a spine whose only check is `pytest -q tests/fixtures/spine_lint/fixture_tests.py -k this_matches_nothing_zzz` (genuinely zero-collect) --
  `python -m scripts.validate_spine <file>`  -> 1 fault (falsifiable-zero-collected) -- correct
  `python3 -m scripts.validate_spine <file>` -> "OK" -- WRONG, a genuinely vacuous check reads as clean

This directly falsifies IMPLEMENTER_RESULT.md's claim under "Behavior changed": "no longer produces interpreter-dependent output -- the same spine file now validates identically regardless of which python on the host ran the checker itself." That claim is true only for `-m pytest`-shaped checks; for bare `pytest` (no `-m`) it is false, on this exact documented host, in the exact `python3 -m scripts.validate_spine` invocation form the round-1 review used to find the original bug.

Mitigating factors against BLOCK: (1) this is not a NEW false positive -- the only explicit auto-BLOCK trigger this handoff names for the fix is "a new false positive anywhere" (w1), and this is a false NEGATIVE; the direction (silence over spurious fault) matches the rework's own stated philosophy ("undecidable is not a failing check"), so it is arguably a narrowing of an existing hazard, not a new one. (2) The corpus sweep (553 files, ~592 pytest-invoking checks) found only 2 bare-`pytest`-shaped commands total, both in old dispatch/harvest archive files, not in the epic's own live spines or shipped templates -- this shape is rare in practice. (3) No regression test in this diff exercises the bare-`pytest`+broken-checker-interpreter combination (TestFalsifiabilityZeroCollectInterpreterUnavailable only constructs `{fake} -m pytest ...` commands), so this gap was never in the tested surface, but its absence from coverage is itself worth naming.

Recording FAIL here (not because it warrants an outright BLOCK on its own -- see consolidation) because the item's own imperative asks for a plain, undownplayed answer: the lint declines to judge a bare `pytest` (no `-m`) command whenever the checker's own runtime lacks pytest importable, and the result doc's blanket interpreter-independence claim is measurably wrong for that shape.

w3-undecidable-is-not-failing.title: How does the lint report what it cannot decide?
w3-undecidable-is-not-failing.imperative: The rework's rule was: an undecidable check is not a failing check. Check what actually happens when pytest is unavailable or the interpreter cannot be resolved -- does the lint stay silent, or does it say it could not tell? Silence and a clean pass look identical to a caller, and this tool's whole purpose is refusing things that look fine. Judge whether the reporting distinguishes 'no fault' from 'could not judge', and whether a caller could act on the difference.
w3-undecidable-is-not-failing.finding:
Traced every return path: `_resolve_interpreter` returns `None` on no-resolve/no-pytest-importable; `_collects_zero` returns `None` (not True/False) when the interpreter can't be resolved, when there's no `-k` selector, or on subprocess OSError/timeout; `_fault_zero_collect` only appends a Fault when `_collects_zero(...)` is truthy (`if _collects_zero(...)`, `None` is falsy) -- so "could not tell" and "checked, found a real test" are collapsed into the exact same code path: no Fault appended, either way. `validate()` returns `list[Fault]` with no companion channel (count of conditions skipped as undecidable, a warning list, anything) -- grepped the whole module for a return path or print that distinguishes the two; none exists outside code comments/docstrings (which are not caller-visible).

Confirmed live via the actual CLI, which is the only interface most callers (spine_amend, a future generator) would use: `main()`'s only branching is `if not faults: print(f"{path}: OK")` vs `print(f"{path}: N fault(s)")`. Ran the CLI against the exact same file with two interpreters that differ only in whether pytest is importable (python vs python3, per w2's reproduction) -- one says "OK", the other says "1 fault(s)". A caller who only reads the CLI's verdict, or only inspects `validate()`'s returned list, cannot tell "this file is sound" from "this file has a check I could not evaluate" -- they read identically. There is no printed/returned signal of "M condition(s) skipped as undecidable" anywhere in the module.

This is exactly the risk the item names: "silence and a clean pass look identical to a caller, and this tool's whole purpose is refusing things that look fine." As built, an operator who runs the checker under the wrong interpreter (the single most likely way to hit this, per CREW_CONTEXT.md's own documented host hazard) gets a false "OK" with zero indication that anything went unevaluated, for a spine that may carry a genuinely vacuous check. The rework's rule ("an undecidable check is not a failing check") is honored in the fault list, but the tool has no way to say "undecidable" at all -- only "fault" or silence, and those two silences (genuinely-clean, and could-not-tell) are indistinguishable to every caller of both the library API and the CLI.

This is the second time this exact script's scope has been wrong (the first time -- over-broad to all of .agent-work/, catching archived epic-298 as a false positive -- the crew already caught and the Admiral already fixed). Recommend a triage candidate: rescope check_corpus_fp.py to the `type`-field methodology, the same fix the crew already applied to the real z3 resweep.

check_corpus_fp.py: NOT a fair statement of "fixed" as currently scoped -- reproduced the exact same class of methodological error the crew's own z3 resweep explicitly identified and avoided in IMPLEMENTER_RESULT.md's own Assumptions section ("a naive PLAN/SPINE-in-filename filter... misclassified non-checklist JSON... not a filename-substring filter, which over- and under-counts"). check_corpus_fp.py's population is `roots = [.agent-work/epic-559, .agent-work/epic-418-followon]` filtered to filenames containing "PLAN" or "SPINE" (case-insensitive) -- exactly that hand-maintained-filename anti-pattern, in the very script whose own comment claims to cover "every spine THIS EPIC drove to a terminal state."

Measured the gap directly: enumerating the SAME two roots by each file's own `type` field (gated/survey), the real population is 25 files, not 14 -- an 11-file, 44% undercount. The 11 silently dropped files include REVIEW_SURVEY.json and REVIEW_SURVEY2.json under a-spine-is-the-job/b-instructions-to-checks/c1-spine-lint (round-1 and round-2 REVIEWER surveys -- exactly the kind of terminal-state artifact the docstring claims to cover), three probe2/*.json fixtures, and five epic-418-followon g1-review/g2-review spine files (execute.json, review.json, review-2/3/4.json). None currently carries a zero-collect fault (checked: 0 of 14 omitted files would flip the exit code today), so the script's PASS/FAIL verdict happens to be right by luck, not by the check's own design -- it "asserts what it examined" (`if seen < 3: REFUSED`, per CREW_CONTEXT.md's loop-assertion rule) but never asserts that what it examined IS the population it claims to model, so a future zero-collect regression landing in any of those 11 files would go completely undetected by this check while it continues to print a clean "examined 14 spine files" / exit 0.

This is the second time this exact script's scope has been wrong (the first time -- over-broad to all of .agent-work/, catching archived epic-298 as a false positive -- the crew already caught and the Admiral already fixed). Say so plainly, per the item's own instruction: 14 files is measurably too narrow to mean what the docstring claims, for a reason (filename-substring filtering) the crew's own work in this same rework already demonstrated is unreliable. Recommend a triage candidate: rescope check_corpus_fp.py to the `type`-field methodology, the same fix the crew already applied to the real z3 resweep.

It is also rare in practice: 2 of ~592 pytest-invoking checks in the full corpus, both in dead archive files, not in this epic's live spines or shipped templates. (3) check_corpus_fp.py is an Admiral-authored script explicitly out of the crew's editing latitude (REWORK_HANDOFF.md: "not yours to edit... block and say so"); its under-scoping does not currently flip its verdict (checked: 0 of the 14 omitted files carry a zero-collect fault today) and is already routed to Triage.
